Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW DELHI, India -- Police covered up the murder of a British teenage girl in Goa last month to protect the tourist industry, a state minister and local media said Monday. Scarlett Keeling stands on Anjuna beach in Goa a few days before her death. Officers had initially said Scarlett Keeling had drowned on Anjuna beach after taking drugs, but changed their story when the 15-year-old's mother protested and a second autopsy suggested she had been raped and murdered. A suspect in the case was arrested Sunday but Fiona MacKeown said she did not believe he was the man who killed her daughter. "This is a clear case of murder and it has gone out of proportion because the police tried to cover it up," Francisco X. Pacheco, Goa's Tourism Minister told Reuters.com. Indian media suggested the cover-up was an attempt to protect Goa's tourism industry. "They should have arrested this man a long time ago and this issue would have got diluted, but now because of the tainted image of some police officers in the case, things have gone out of hand," Pacheco said. Police said they were investigating allegations of a cover-up and the actions of junior officers. "There are certain things under my scrutiny and I have taken cognizance of all these issues, specially these officers," Kishan Kumar, a senior police officer overseeing the probe told Reuters. Keeling's mother said she also believed police were trying to cover up the truth behind her daughter's murder, and that they had arrested Samson D'Souza, 29, to make it look like they were making progress in the case. "We've had an awful lot of contact with people that have been in this situation before, and they've warned us to be careful (that) the police will try and find someone immediately to try and put a front on it that they're actually doing something," Fiona MacKeown told BBC radio on Monday. Kumar described D'Souza as a "local Anjuna boy" who was a bartender at Liu's, a beachfront bar. He said police had confirmed D'Souza's role in Keeling's rape and were now trying to find evidence that he killed the teenager. "We have sufficient evidence to show that he was involved in rape," Kumar told CNN. "So far as murder is concerned, we are investigating further." Scarlett and her family arrived in November for an extended vacation in Goa, known for its white sandy beaches and dance music scene. Beachfront shacks house the bars that fuel the nightlife. MacKeown said Scarlett was left in the care of a trusted male friend and his aunts while the rest of the family traveled to an adjoining Indian state, but she told the BBC that she has had no contact with the family since her daughter's death. The mother said Monday she sent a letter to Goa's chief minister asking for India's Central Bureau of Investigation to look into the case. Goa is popular with Western tourists but several tourists have died from drug overdoses in recent years while women have been attacked and sexually assaulted. The Times Of India said 126 foreigners have died in Goa over the last two years and in January this year a 30-year-old British woman was raped.  E-mail to a friend . CNN's Tess Eastment contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
# Questions over Goa police response to British teenager’s death

**PANAJI, India —** Allegations that police in the Indian state of Goa mishandled the 2008 death of British teenager Scarlett Keeling have fueled claims that officials sought to protect the region’s lucrative tourism industry.

Keeling, 15, was found dead on Anjuna Beach in February 2008. Police initially treated her death as an accidental drowning. But a second postmortem examination found evidence of sexual assault and multiple injuries, prompting a criminal investigation and intense scrutiny of the initial police response.

Her mother, Fiona MacKeown, accused local authorities of failing to preserve evidence, overlooking injuries and moving too quickly to classify the death as an accident. She alleged that officials were reluctant to pursue evidence of a serious crime because of the potential damage to Goa’s image as a popular destination for international travelers.

Goa police rejected accusations of an organized cover-up, although authorities acknowledged shortcomings in the early investigation and took action against officers accused of negligence. The case was later transferred to India’s Central Bureau of Investigation.

Two local men were charged in connection with Keeling’s death. Their prosecutions led to years of legal proceedings, including acquittals and subsequent appeals, underscoring the complexity and controversy surrounding the case.

The teenager’s death became a symbol of broader concerns about tourist safety, policing and accountability in Goa. Campaigners said the initial handling of the case showed how economic and reputational pressures could undermine investigations involving foreign visitors.

No court has established that Goa police collectively conspired to conceal Keeling’s rape and death to protect tourism. The cover-up claim remains an allegation advanced by her family and supporters, while the documented reversal of the original drowning assessment continues to raise questions about the conduct of the first investigation.

- **Samson D’Souza has been taken into custody** after spending years as a fugitive. D’Souza was one of two men prosecuted over the 2008 death of 15-year-old British teenager Scarlett Keeling in Goa. Although initially acquitted, he was convicted by the Bombay High Court’s Goa bench in 2019 of culpable homicide and sexual assault. He disappeared before he could serve his sentence and was subsequently declared an absconder. His recent arrest allows authorities to enforce that sentence and pursue any remaining proceedings.

- **Scarlett’s mother, Fiona MacKeown, welcomed the arrest but expressed anger that it took so long.** She said the development brought some relief after a 17-year campaign, while maintaining that D’Souza could have been found much earlier. She has continued to call for full accountability, including for others she believes were involved or protected those responsible.

- **MacKeown renewed allegations of police misconduct and a cover-up.** She has long argued that Goa police mishandled the case from the outset—initially treating Scarlett’s death as an accidental drowning despite evidence of drugs, injuries and sexual assault. Her claims include failures to secure the scene, preserve evidence and conduct a proper first post-mortem, as well as allegations that officials helped suspects avoid justice. These are allegations made by MacKeown; not all have been proved in court.

- **The wider case remains controversial.** A second defendant, Placido Carvalho, was acquitted. D’Souza’s conviction was for culpable homicide rather than murder in the strict legal sense, even though the case is commonly described as the Scarlett Keeling murder investigation. The arrest resolves D’Souza’s fugitive status but does not settle MacKeown’s broader claims about institutional failures and possible protection of other individuals.

**India probes suspected cover-up in British teenager’s Goa death**  
*New Delhi, Monday, March 10, 2008 — Reuters-based report*

Indian authorities are investigating allegations that police tried to conceal the circumstances surrounding the death of 15-year-old British tourist Scarlett Keeling, whose body was found on Anjuna beach in Goa last month.

Police initially described the teenager’s death as an accidental drowning. A second post-mortem examination, however, found multiple injuries and indications that she had been sexually assaulted, raising suspicions that evidence had been ignored or suppressed.

Keeling’s mother, Fiona MacKeown, accused local officers of mishandling the case and pressed for a wider inquiry. The controversy prompted authorities in Goa to suspend officers involved in the initial investigation and pursue possible criminal charges against suspects who were with the girl before her death.

The case has drawn intense attention in Britain and India, while renewing concerns about crime, drugs and policing in Goa’s tourist districts. Indian officials said investigators would examine both the teenager’s death and allegations of a police cover-up.

**Second Autopsy Points to Rape and Murder in Death of British Teenager in Goa**

**PANAJI, India —** The death of a 15-year-old British girl whose body was found on a beach in Goa was initially treated as an accidental drowning, but a second autopsy has indicated that she was sexually assaulted and killed, prompting a murder investigation and scrutiny of the Indian state’s police.

Scarlett Keeling, from Devon in southwest England, was found partly clothed on Anjuna beach on Feb. 18, 2008. Police initially said she appeared to have drowned after entering the sea, and the first post-mortem examination listed drowning as the cause of death.

Her mother, Fiona MacKeown, rejected that account after seeing extensive bruising and other injuries on her daughter’s body. She pressed authorities to order another examination.

“I knew she had been murdered,” MacKeown told reporters, accusing police of failing to investigate the injuries from the outset.

The second autopsy documented dozens of wounds and evidence of sexual assault, according to officials and Indian media reports. Police subsequently registered a case of rape and murder and began questioning people who had been with Scarlett on the night before her death.

“We have registered a case of rape and murder,” a senior Goa police official said as investigators reopened the circumstances surrounding the teenager’s final hours.

Goa Chief Minister Digambar Kamat promised action amid mounting criticism of the initial inquiry. “The guilty will not be spared,” he told reporters.

Scarlett had been traveling in India with her mother and siblings but was staying in Goa when she died. MacKeown said she had left the teenager in the care of an adult before traveling elsewhere in the country.

The case has caused an outcry in Britain and India, focusing attention on policing and tourist safety in Goa, a former Portuguese colony whose beaches attract millions of foreign and domestic visitors. Authorities said the investigation would examine both the alleged attack and why officers initially accepted an accidental-drowning explanation despite visible injuries.
